parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *-s, either reduced from *-kse (translative ending): *-kse > *-ks > *-s, or alternatively from Proto-Uralic *-s (compare Erzya -с (-s) in эйс (ejs, “into”)).

parole.significato: Forms nouns, indicating resemblance or association.
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *-us. Probably generalized from -s-derivatives of u-stem nominals (e.g. etu- → edus, palvelu → palvelus), or through the loss of a plain u-derivative from the standard language (e.g. keski- → dial. kesku- → keskus), and thus identical to -us (etymology 1). In some cases potentially

parole.significato: Forms an adjective from a noun.
parole.testo: Two theories exist: * Of the same origin as the participle ending above (etymology 1), with the same levelling of the weak grade (*-ba). * Alternatively, from Proto-Finnic *-va, from Proto-Uralic *-ŋa.

From Proto-Finnic *ahma (“glutton”) (compare dialectal Estonian ahm (“glutton”), Ingrian ahmo (“greedy”), Karelian ahmo (“wolverine, glutton”), Ludian ahmo (“wolverine”)), probably ultimately borrowed from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Haćman- (compare Sanskrit अश्मन् (aśman, “eater”)). Related also to Proto-

From Proto-Finnic *aivan (an instructive singular, compare ihan), probably borrowed from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Háywas, or alternatively from Proto-Germanic *aiwaz (“long time”). Cognate with Votic aiva (“always”) and Estonian aiva (“always”).

From Proto-Finnic *akkuna (compare Estonian aken), borrowed from Old East Slavic окъно (okŭno) (whence also Russian окно́ (oknó)) or from earlier Slavic, from Proto-Slavic *okъno. Compare Udmurt укно (ukno) (borrowed from the aforementioned Russian word).

parole.significato: a plant of the genus Filipendula
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *angër-, possibly borrowed from Proto-Baltic [Term?] (whence Lithuanian vangarykštė) or alternatively from a hypothetical Proto-Norse [script needed] (*angan-wahstuʀ).
From Proto-Finnic *aukko (compare Estonian auk, Votic aukko), either derived from the same root as avata, aukea, or alternatively proposed to be a borrowing from Proto-Germanic *augô (“eye”).

Formed with the suffix -nko from a root of unknown origin, which has been proposed, among others, to derive from auer (thus from earlier *auderinko),from a Baltic language (compare Lithuanian aušrà (“dawn”)), or according to Saarikivi (2022), possibly from Old Norse Aurvandill. Alternatively origina
Borrowed either from North Germanic (compare Old Norse enda) or from Middle Low German ende, in either case ultimately from Proto-Germanic *anþi. Compare Estonian ent (“but”).
Ultimately from Italian grottesco, probably through French grotesque, either directly or through German grotesk (as suggested by the Finnish pronunciation) or Swedish grotesk.

Probably from Proto-Finnic *hagastadak, derived from unattested *haka (“quarrel, legal matter”) (earlier *šaka), borrowed from Proto-Germanic *sakō. Alternatively, borrowed from Proto-Baltic [Term?] (compare Lithuanian žósti (“to say”)). Related to Karelian hoastoa.

parole.significato: fluff of wool; tuft of wool to be spun; rolag
parole.testo: From hahtu + -va, the shorter form being derivative of either Proto-Finnic *hapci (thus from earlier *haptu) or alternatively a borrowing from Proto-Germanic *hazdaz (thus from earlier *haštu).

Uncertain, but proposed to be a Baltic loan (whence Lithuanian žaizda (“wound”)), or alternatively possibly from earlier *hagitta and then from Proto-Norse *hagiþō, compare Swedish hejd. Cognate with Karelian haitta.

parole.significato: swidden; farmland that is produced using the slash and burn technique
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *halmëh, borrowed from either Proto-Germanic *halmaz or alternatively Proto-Baltic [Term?] (whence Lithuanian želmuo). Cognate with Estonian ale, Karelian halmeh, Ludian halmeh and Veps haumeh.
Borrowed either from Swedish handske (“glove”) or directly from Middle Low German hantsche.
From Proto-Finnic *harakka ~ *haraga, possibly of onomatopoeic origin, or alternatively borrowed from Proto-Balto-Slavic *śárˀkāˀ.
Borrowed either from Swedish harmonika (or alternatively from Russian гармо́ника (garmónika)), ultimately from Latin harmonica.

parole.significato: skirt, base, lap (part of a dress or robe, etc., that hangs below the waist)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *hëlma (compare Estonian hõlm), possibly borrowed either from Baltic (compare Lithuanian šelmuo (“ridge (of a roof)”)) or from Proto-Germanic *helmaz (“protective covering”) (compare Old English helm (“helmet, protection, covering”)).
From Proto-Finnic *helbeh, borrowed from Proto-Germanic [Term?] (whence Old High German helwa, helawa), or alternatively a more recent Germanic borrowing.

A genitive or instructive singular form of *hiema, which could be from Proto-Finnic *hëëma-, possibly borrowed from Proto-Germanic *sēmô through earlier *šeema(n) (in which case the word is a doublet of siemen), or alternatively derived from hieta through irregular suffix substitution. However, neit

parole.significato: reindeer stag (adult male reindeer, sometimes defined as one that is at least three years old)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *hirvas, borrowed from Proto-Balto-Slavic *śirwas. Cognate with Northern Sami sarvvis, which must have either been borrowed directly from Balto-Slavic or (more likely) come via Finnic before *š became h. Doublet of sarvas.
Possibly derived from Russian ходить (xoditʹ) or from a Germanic root (compare Old High German huota) + -e.
From Proto-Finnic *huilu, probably onomatopoeic or alternatively (from earlier *šuilu and) borrowed from Proto-Germanic *sweglō.

From Proto-Finnic *huima (compare Estonian uim, Ingrian huima), probably borrowed from Proto-Germanic [Term?] (compare Old Norse svíma (“to faint, to swoon”)) or Proto-Norse [Term?] (compare Old Norse hvima (“to be confused”)); for sense, compare huimata. Alternatively, possibly akin to huikea (comp

parole.significato: headscarf, scarf (piece of cloth worn over the head)
parole.testo: Borrowed from dialectal Swedish hviv (“women's headwear, bride's veil”) or from earlier Old Swedish hviver.

parole.significato: To make a loud sound with one's voice.
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *huutadak (compare Estonian hüüdma, Ingrian huutaa), either onomatopoeic, or alternatively a borrowing from Proto-Norse [script needed] (*hūta) (compare Gutnish huti (“to yell, to scream”)). * (to bid in an auction): Originally bids were shouted at auctions.

From Proto-Finnic *hämärä, derived from a root hämä-, which may be possibly borrowed from Proto-Germanic [Term?] (compare Icelandic sámur) or from Baltic. Related to Estonian hämar, Karelian hämärä, Livonian ämār, Veps hämär and Votic hämäre.

From Proto-Finnic *iha (compare Estonian iha), probably borrowed from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hišćáti (“to wish, desire, seek”) (whence Sanskrit इच्छति (iccháti)) or from Proto-Indo-Iranian *Hiš (compare Avestan 𐬍𐬱 (īš)).

parole.significato: A type of small sailing boat.
parole.testo: From English yawl, either through Russian ял (jal) or Swedish jala.

parole.significato: group, cluster, band; crowd (of people) (number of things or persons, especially a rather large and unorganized one)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *joukko, borrowed from Proto-Germanic *jaukiją or from older Proto-Indo-European *yewg- (see the Proto-Finnic entry for more).

Late Old Swedish iudhe + -lainen, or more directly from Latin iūdaeus or Ancient Greek Ῐ̓ουδαῖος (Ĭoudaîos) with the same suffix; -a- may also be influenced by Juudas (“Judas”); alternatively, derived from the common noun juudas, juutas (“Jew”) (from the aforementioned Latin/Greek word) found in Old

From Proto-Finnic *järvi (compare Estonian järv), from Proto-Finno-Permic *jäwrä (compare Northern Sami jávri, Erzya эрьке (eŕke)), probably borrowed from Indo-European, either from Proto-Balto-Slavic *jáuˀrāˀ (compare Lithuanian jáura (“marshland, bog”)) or from earlier Proto-Indo-European *yewHr-.

parole.significato: thick, dry and hard bark, such as that of a pine
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *karna, borrowed either from Baltic *karna- or alternatively Proto-Norse [script needed] (*skarna) (in which case related to English shear and Swedish skära).

From Proto-Finnic *kaktëksa, from Proto-Finno-Permic *kakteksa (cognate with Erzya кавксо (kavkso), Moksha кафкса (kafksa)). The initial component is kaksi (“two”), but the nature of the latter component (shared with yhdeksän (“nine”)) remains disputed (see the Proto-Finno-Permic entry for more). Th

From Proto-Finnic *kahlëh, cognate with Karelian kahleh (“shackle, burden”), Ingrian kahle. Proposed to be either a further development of kahle (etymology 2), or alternatively derived from Germanic (compare haahla (“trammel hook”) from Proto-Germanic *hanhlō).

Probably from Proto-Finnic *kalppa, borrowed by metathesis from Proto-Germanic *glapa- (whence Icelandic glapp (“misfortune”) and Old Norse glap (“fornication, impropriety”)). Alternatively, possibly akin to kalpea, with development like “pale” → “ugly” → “bad”. In either case, with + -ten.

From Proto-Finnic *kamala (compare Ingrian kamala, Karelian kamala, Votic kamalõ), possibly borrowed from Proto-Germanic *hamalaz. Alternatively, possibly related to Erzya кама- (kama-) in камажа (kamaža, “bad”).
From Swedish kanel, from either Italian cannella, French cannelle or a cognate of such. In either case the ultimate root word is Latin canna.

From Proto-Finnic *kangar, *kankarëh, probably from Proto-Norse [script needed] (*gangaʀ), a later loan from the same source as kangas (“a soil type with moraine”); alternatively possibly from Proto-Uralic *këŋka- (“to climb”) (compare kangertaa). Related to Estonian kangur, Karelian kankareh and Li

parole.significato: to limb, delimb (to remove the branches of a tree)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *karcidak, borrowed from Proto-Germanic *skardijaną, or alternatively from Baltic (compare Lithuanian skardyti).
From Proto-Finnic *karcina, probably borrowed from Proto-Baltic [Term?] (compare Lithuanian gardinys) or alternatively from Germanic.

parole.significato: a type of boat used to drag a seine
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *karbas, probably borrowed from Proto-Norse [Term?] (compare Old Norse karfi), or alternatively and less likely from Baltic (compare Lithuanian kãrbas).

parole.significato: saucepan (deep, and usually rather small, cooking vessel with a handle)
parole.testo: Unknown. Possibly from Swedish kastrull or from Russian казан (kazan).
Borrowed from Swedish kasarm, from older German Kasarme, from Italian caserma, either from French caserne or its source Old Occitan cazerna.

parole.significato: to do, work, suffice, be good enough
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *këlbat'ak (compare Estonian kõlbama), borrowed from Pre-Germanic *kelp- (“help”) (from Proto-Indo-European *ḱelb-, *ḱelp- and whence Proto-Germanic *helpaną, compare English help, Swedish hjälpa), or alternatively borrowed from Baltic (compare Lithuanian gelbėti).

parole.significato: Wednesday (day of the week; the third day of the week in Finland and in the ISO 8601 standard)
parole.testo: keski- (“mid-, middle”) + viikko (“week”), a calque either of Middle Low German middewēke (compare modern German Mittwoch), or of a seemingly unattested Old Swedish word (compare Old Norse miðvikudagr (literally “mid-week day”)). Note that Wednesday was the middle of the seven-day week when Sunday w

parole.significato: to stand, withstand, endure, hold up (to), stand up (to)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *kestädäk (compare Estonian kestma), possibly either borrowed from Baltic (compare Lithuanian kę̃sti) or alternatively derived from keski-.

parole.significato: bow, prow (front of a boat or ship)
parole.testo: Possibly from Proto-Finnic *këula, possibly borrowed from Proto-Germanic *skeulą (“shelter”) or alternatively Proto-Germanic *keulaz (“ship”). Alternatively from Proto-Finnic *këpla, possibly borrowed from Proto-Germanic *geblą.
From Proto-Finnic *kiivas, borrowed from Proto-Baltic *gīˀwás or alternatively from Proto-Germanic *kwiwaz (“lively, quick”), both from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós.
Either from Swedish klisché or directly from French cliché.
Probably from Proto-Slavic *košь (“basket”), possibly via Proto-Samic *kuoššē. Alternatively and less likely, according to UEW, from Proto-Uralic *koća.

Borrowed either from Old Swedish gumme (“man”) (compare Swedish gumma) or from Russian кум (kum, “godfather”), кума́ (kumá, “godmother”) (compare Latvian kūma (“godparent”), Latvian kūmas (“godparent”)).

parole.significato: to well (up/forth), spring (up/forth) (e.g. of water or some other liquid matter)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *kumbut'ak, probably from Proto-Uralic *kumpa- (“to surge, move in waves”). Alternatively, from kummu- + -ta.
Possibly from Old East Slavic кумъ (kumŭ, “godfather”) (compare Old East Slavic кума (kuma, “godmother”), Polish kum). Alternatively borrowed from Sami, compare Northern Sami guoibmi.
From Proto-Finnic *kura (“dirt, mud”) (compare Estonian kura), possibly borrowed from Proto-Germanic *gurą or alternatively from Proto-Uralic *kura (“dirt, mud”).

parole.significato: to strangle, choke, throttle (constrict someone's windpipe so that they cannot breathe)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *kurgistadak, probably borrowed from Proto-Germanic *kwirkijaną. Alternatively, and less likely, related to kuroa.

parole.significato: common European adder (Vipera berus, the only natural species of viper in Finland)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *küü (compare Estonian küü), possibly from Proto-Uralic *kije (compare Erzya гуй (guj), Moksha куй (kuj), Hungarian kígyó), or alternatively an old clipping for kyykäärme (see the Proto-Finnic entry for more).
From Proto-Finnic *käki, either a Baltic loanword or alternatively an onomatopoeia. Related to Estonian kägu, Karelian käki, Livonian kä’g, Veps kägi, Votic čako and Northern Sami giehka.

From Proto-Finnic *kärsä, possibly an Indo-Iranian loan. Alternatively, possibly from Sami, compare Northern Sami gearsi (“pig's snout”) (from Proto-Samic *kearsē, cognate with kehrä). Related to kirsu.

parole.significato: French toast, usually served as dessert with strawberry jam and whipped cream
parole.testo: köyhät (“poor”) + ritarit (“knights”); a calque, either of Swedish fattiga riddare (“poor knights”) or German Arme Ritter (“poor knights”) - also in England a dessert of French toasts with jam has been called the poor knights of Windsor.

From Proto-Finnic *lakja (compare Estonian lai, Livonian laigā, Votic ladʹdʹõ), borrowed from Germanic, either Proto-Germanic *flakją (compare German flach) or alternatively *lēgijaz (compare laakea).
Borrowed from Russian лад (lad) or from earlier Old East Slavic ладъ (ladŭ). Cognate with Estonian laad.

parole.significato: sect (offshoot of a larger religion sharing at least some unorthodox beliefs)
parole.testo: Partly from Proto-Finnic *lahko (compare Estonian lahk, Livonian lǭ’gõ, Veps lahk), borrowed either from Proto-Germanic *slagiz or Proto-Germanic *slahō. The original sense inherited from Finnic is “split log”, which is found only in some eastern Finnish dialects in the form laahko. Partly borrowed

Borrowed from Late Old Swedish lakan, from Late Old Norse lak, lakan, from Old Saxon lakan, from Proto-Germanic *lakaną (“sheet, cloth”); alternatively directly from either Old Saxon lakan, or an older Germanic loan.
Either from Swedish or Russian лаке́й (lakéj), originally from French.

parole.significato: paralysis, depression (state of being unable to act)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *lama (compare Estonian lamama (“to lie down”), Ludian lama, Votic lama), borrowed from Proto-Germanic *lamaz (“lame, withered; defective”). Alternatively related to Moksha лама (lama) and Erzya ламо (lamo, “many”), although the semantic shift is problematic.

parole.significato: to discourage, demoralise/demoralize, dispirit, dishearten, push down, demotivate
parole.testo: According to Aikio (2026), from Proto-Finnic [Term?] (compare dialectal lantua, lanttua (“to languish, collapse due to exhaustion, pass out”)), from Proto-Uralic *lëmtɜ- (“to stoop down”) (whence also Proto-Samic *luomtētēk (“to lie down and refuse to get up”), Erzya ландямс (lanďams, “to crouch dow

From Proto-Finnic *laskëdak (compare Estonian laskma), from Proto-Uralic *lëćke- (compare Erzya ластямс (lasťams, “to saddle”), Moksha ласькомс (laśkoms, “to run”)). Semantic development * (to lower, drop, put down): Inherited from at least Proto-Finnic. *: → (to bring down, decrease): Figurative de

From Proto-Finnic *lauha, of unclear further etymology; either related to Erzya лавшо (lavšo, “weak”), or alternatively borrowed from Proto-Germanic *lausaz (compare Swedish lös) or Proto-Germanic *hlāwaz (variant of *hlēwaz).

From Proto-Finnic *lausudak, possibly borrowed from Proto-Baltic [Term?] (whence Lithuanian klausti), or alternatively possibly from laus- (“loose”) + -ua (hence "to let loose, let forth"). Cognate with Estonian lause, lausuma.

parole.significato: board (long, wide and thin piece of sawn timber)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *lauta (compare Estonian laud (“table”)), most likely borrowed from Proto-Baltic *plauˀtá (compare Latvian plàukts, Lithuanian plaũtas (“shelf”)), or alternatively from Proto-Germanic *flauþī (compare Norwegian Nynorsk flauta (“crossbeam in sleigh”)). The word has also been borrowe

parole.significato: to sail (to move briskly and gracefully through the air)
parole.testo: Possibly borrowed from Proto-Germanic *glīdaną, either as an old borrowing (into Proto-Finnic *liitädäk) or a more recent one (such as from Swedish glida). Cognate with Karelian liiteä.

Unknown, but related to Northern Sami luopma. Possibly from luoda. Alternatively, according to Rahkonen (2017), possibly borrowed from dialectal Estonian loom (“riverbend”), originally in the sense "bend, draught"; the Estonian word may then derive from Baltic (compare Lithuanian lomà (“lowland, dep

parole.significato: A recurring pain in limbs; could mean several diseases, most probably gout.
parole.testo: luu (“bone”) + valo (“pain (archaic)”), latter part from Proto-Finnic *valo (“pain”), either borrowed from Proto-Germanic *kwalō or less likely from *valo (“light”).

parole.significato: Monday (day of the week; the first day of the week in Finland and in the ISO 8601 standard)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish mānadagher, or from Middle Low German māndach; ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *mānini dag.
Possibly from Swedish man or German Mann, found in many Swedish and German names used by the Finnish Romani community. Alternatively, from the name Herman.

parole.significato: mainland (main landmass of a country, continent or sometimes of a group of islands)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *mandër, from Proto-Finno-Permic [Term?] or possibly from Proto-Finnic *maa. Equivalent to *mante- + -re. Cognate to Estonian mander and Veps mandreh.
Probably borrowed from German marsch!, French marche!, or alternatively and less likely, an irregular imperative form of marssia (compare seis < seistä).

parole.significato: in doing something with someone else, in a group doing something
parole.testo: Inessive singular of messi-, either from Swedish med (perhaps med sig, sounding like messej in rapid speech), or from Russian вместе (vmeste).
From Proto-Finnic *mëtu, borrowed either from Proto-Balto-Slavic *medú or alternatively Proto-Germanic *meduz. Cognate with Estonian mõdu, Võro mõdu and Votic mõtu.

Most likely borrowed from Swedish mor in the same way as faija from Swedish far. Alternatively, from dialectal Swedish mója (compare moja sig). First mentioned in a dictionary in 1786 as muuja, in its current form in 1823. Swedish moja may however be borrowed from Finnish due to its narrow distribut
From Proto-Finnic *mura, probably from the same Proto-Uralic *mura- (“to break”) as murtaa, or alternatively from Proto-Germanic [Term?] (compare Icelandic mor).

parole.significato: ant (insect of the family Formicidae); (in the plural) the family Formicidae
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *muurahainën, borrowed either from Proto-Germanic *miurijǭ (compare Swedish myra), or from its source Proto-Indo-European *morwi- (compare Russian мураве́й (muravéj), Ukrainian мура́ха (muráxa), Polish mrówka). Contains a diminutive -(i)nen.

parole.significato: tacky, sticky, especially because it is (slightly) wet (like wet leather)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *nahkëda, probably derived from Proto-Finno-Ugric *ńëčke (“wet”) or alternatively from nahka; see the Proto-Finnic entry for more.
From Proto-Finnic *napa, borrowed from Proto-Baltic [Term?], or alternatively and less likely from Proto-Germanic *nabō, but in either case ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nebʰ- (“navel”).
Either napa + kaira, formed after Proto-Norse *ᚾᚨᛒᛟᚷᚨᛁᛉᚨᛉ (*nabogaiʀaʀ) (from Proto-Germanic *nabōgaizaz), or directly borrowed from it.

parole.significato: rhinitis, "sniffles" (inflammation of the mucous membranes of the nose, leading to a runny or congested nose)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *nuha, probably borrowed from Proto-Germanic *snuzaz (whence Swedish snor) or alternatively, from Proto-Germanic *hnuzô (whence Icelandic hnerri).
From Proto-Finnic *noodëh (albeit without any known Finnic cognates), either borrowed from Baltic (compare Latvian znots) or alternatively from Proto-Germanic *knōdiz.

From Proto-Finnic *noori (“young”) (compare Estonian noor), probably from either Proto-Uralic *ńëre (“moist, wet; flexible, pliable”) (compare Northern Sami njuoras, Erzya and Moksha нар (nar, “weed, grass”), Udmurt нюр (ńur, “bog, swamp”), Northern Mansi [script needed] (ńār), Hungarian nyirkos, Tu
From Proto-Finnic *ocra, borrowed either from Proto-Baltic *aśras (“sharp”) or from Proto-Iranian *Hacra-. Cognates include Estonian oder, Ingrian odra, Karelian osra, Veps ozr.

Possibly borrowed from Middle Low German ovel, ovele, from Proto-Germanic *ubilaz. Alternatively related to dialectal evelä, Estonian õel (“wicked, cruel, savage, evil, mean”) and Votic õjõla (Pummala).
From Proto-Finnic *palvodak, possibly borrowed from Baltic. Cognate with Estonian paluma and Livonian pallõ (“to ask for”). Alternatively related to Erzya паламс (palams, “kiss”).
From Proto-Finnic *parta, borrowed from either Proto-Baltic *bardā́ˀ, Proto-Germanic *bardaz or Proto-Slavic *bordà, in any case ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰardʰéh₂.

From Proto-Finnic *parvi, possibly related to parvi (etymology 1), perhaps originally in the sense "group of logs joined together", or from a separate Proto-Uralic root. Cognates include Estonian parv (“raft”), Ingrian parvi (“shelf, balcony”), Northern Khanty пөр (pør, “raft”) and Tundra Nenets [sc

From Proto-Finnic *peijeh + -as, either from Proto-Indo-Iranian *paHiyas (“libation”) or alternatively and less likely from Proto-Germanic *faigijaz (“fey, doomed to die”), compare Old Norse feigr (“near to death”). Cognate with Estonian peied (“wake”).

parole.significato: goblin, hobgoblin, gnome, gremlin (mythical man-like creature, often depicted hairy, tailed and mischievous)
parole.testo: From older peikkoi, from Proto-Finnic *peikoi, *peiko (reshaped later with -kko; compare Estonian peig (“bridegroom”)), deriving either from Proto-Germanic *faihaz (“hostile, criminal”), *faigijaz (“fey”), or alternatively from a lost Baltic cognate (inexact parallels include Lithuanian paikas (“stu

parole.significato: Friday (day of the week; the fifth day of the week in Finland and in the ISO 8601 standard)
parole.testo: Borrowed from North Germanic, probably Old Swedish frē(i)adagher, frīadagher; ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *Frījā dag. Details Since Finnish historically lacks f and initial consonant clusters (such as fr), the word was adapted to fit the language's phonological rules, with f- becoming p- and

parole.significato: pot (money in center of table in card games)
parole.testo: From Swedish pott. Sense "poker (in card games)" either a calque of or directly from English pot.

Probably from French brouille, brouillon (“sketch, notes”), possibly through Russian [Term?], originally through Helsinki slang. Alternatively borrowed from Russian сбруя (sbruja, “horse tack; instrument, tool”) (accusative: сбрую (sbruju)), compare mortu (“face”, obsolete, Viipuri slang)).

parole.significato: feral pigeon (Columba livia, syn. Columba livia domestica)
parole.testo: Either of onomatopoeic origin, or from Swedish pull, pulla, from French poule.

parole.significato: sail; (colloquial) rag, sheet (piece of fabric attached to a boat and arranged such that it causes the wind to drive th…
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *purjëh, probably borrowed from Proto-Germanic *buriz (“favourable wind”), or alternatively and less likely from Baltic (compare Lithuanian burė, Latvian bura). The Baltic words have also sometimes been proposed to be Finnic loans.

parole.significato: milk can (metal container for carrying small amounts of milk, typically for domestic use)
parole.testo: Either directly from dialectal (Finnish) Swedish pejlare, or somehow irregularly derived from Swedish bära (“to carry, bear”), in which case the aforementioned dialectal word has been reborrowed from Finnish.
From Proto-Finnic *rakja, borrowed from either a Germanic or alternatively a Baltic language.

parole.significato: jury, panel (body of judges in a competition)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old Swedish rāþ (compare modern Swedish råd (“council”), German Rat (“council”)) or from Middle Low German rāt. Doublet of roti.

parole.significato: stripe, band (long strip of a colour or material)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Proto-Norse [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *raidō, originally referring to a trail or track left behind while riding. Association with raita (etymology 2) has also been proposed. Cognate with Northern Karelian raita. Related to raide, either a derivative or a parallel loan from the same
From Proto-Finnic *rak'ëntadak, either borrowed from Proto-Germanic *rakjaną or inherited from Proto-Finno-Ugric *rakkɜ-.
From Proto-Finnic *rampa, borrowed from Proto-Norse [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *krampaz (“curved”), or from Proto-Baltic [Term?]. If the former, doublet of kremppa.

parole.significato: shore, strand, coast (the border of a body of water and land in general)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *ranta (compare Estonian rand, Veps rand), borrowed from either Proto-Norse [script needed] (*stranða), Proto-Germanic *strandō (compare Swedish strand (“beach”)) or from Proto-Baltic *kranta (compare Lithuanian krantas (“beach, shore”)).
Either from Swedish griffel or Russian гри́фель (grífelʹ), both from German Griffel.

From Proto-Finnic *rindeh, probably from rinta (“chest, breast”) + -e, or alternatively (if from Proto-Finnic *rindek) possibly borrowed from Proto-Germanic [Term?] (whence Norwegian strind (“strip, half, row, edge”) or rind (“esker, stripe in cloth”)).
From either Swedish rips or German Rips (German Ripsbindung), ultimately from French reps.

From Proto-Finnic *rohkëda (compare Estonian rohke, Ingrian rohkia, Karelian rohkei, Veps rohked), from earlier *rošketa, possibly borrowed from a Germanic language (compare Proto-Germanic *raskuz, Old Norse rǫskr), or alternatively from the same root as rohtia.
From Proto-Finnic *roodëh, probably borrowed from Proto-Germanic [Term?] (whence Old Norse tróð (“thatch, roof beam, rafter”)). Alternatively, possibly from ruoto + -e.
Probably borrowed from Middle Low German brôk with + -e; alternatively, an older borrowing from Proto-Germanic *brōks (implying Proto-Finnic *rook'ëh).

From Proto-Finnic *ruskëda, ultimately probably from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rowdʰ-s-o- or *rudʰ-s-to- via some Indo-European language, either Baltic, Germanic or Slavic; see the Proto-Finnic entry for more.

parole.significato: to sip, to drink, to toss off (have a drink)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *rüüp'ät'äk. Cognate to Estonian rüüpama. Possibly onomatopoeic; alternatively a loan from Proto-Germanic *dreupaną.
Borrowed from Old Swedish sagh, or possibly already from Proto-Norse [Term?] (compare maha), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *sagō.

parole.significato: a handle for carrying, particularly one that is relatively thin but stiff, e.g. made of metal wire or another similar m…
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *sanka, possibly from Proto-Finno-Permic *ćanka (compare Erzya сянго (śango)) and borrowed from Indo-Iranian, or alternatively possibly borrowed from Proto-Germanic *stangō.

From Proto-Finnic *se, either from Proto-Uralic *śe or Proto-Finno-Permic *śej. For plural forms, see etymology of ne. The variation in inflectional stems (se-, si-, sii-) dates back to at least Late Proto-Finnic; see the Proto-Finnic entry for more.

parole.significato: cheque, check (note promising to pay money to a named person or entity)
parole.testo: From English check through either French chèque or Swedish check.
Unknown. Possibly an irregular blend of selvitä + vatvoa, a derivation from Russian сеть (setʹ, “net”), сетево́й (setevój), or from Russian четверть (četvertʹ).

Possibly from Swedish seka (“to be slow”) + -illa. The Swedish word is dialectal and related to seckla (“to drool”). Alternatively a Sami borrowing (compare Northern Sami čiehkat (“to hide, conceal”)).

Uncertain. Possibly from Proto-Finnic *seevä, from Proto-Finno-Permic *ćejŋe ~ *ćijŋe (“jewellery, ornament”) (whence Northern Sami čikŋa (“piece of jewellery; ornament, decoration”), Erzya сия (sija, “silver”) and Eastern Mari ший (šij, “silver”). Alternatively, possibly irregularly derived from si

Possibly borrowed from Swedish sillake, from sill (“herring”) + lake (“brine”) (compare saltlake), referring to the brine herrings were salted with, in which case the original meaning was “salted herring” (indeed found in some dialects). The word may have been influenced by salakka, another word for

Ultimately from Italian soldato, either from: * Swedish soldat + -ski, a pseudo-Russian suffix; compare the synonymous soldari, solttu, and for the suffix, flikuski; * or a syncopic form of Russian солдатушки (soldatuški, “little soldiers”), from Russian солдат (soldat).

parole.significato: Stradivarius (stringed instrument built by members of the Stradivari family, particularly Antonio Stradivari)
parole.testo: Named after the Stradivari family (Latin Stradivarius), an Italian surname either from the plural of Lombard stradivare (“toll-man”), or from strada averta (“open road”) in the Cremonese dialect.

parole.significato: large, big, great (of considerable size or extent)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *suuri, borrowed either from Proto-Germanic *stūraz or from Proto-Indo-Iranian *stʰuHrás (see the Proto-Finnic entry for more).

parole.significato: to get angry, get annoyed, get upset
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *suuttudak, probably derived from early Proto-Slavic *sūtu (later *sytъ). Alternatively from suu (“mouth”) + -ttua. Compare suivaantua.

parole.significato: stream pool (stretch of a river or stream in which the water depth is above average and the water velocity is quite bel…
parole.testo: Possibly syvä + -nto. While this would require a seemingly irregular shift from front into back vowels, the front-vowel variant syväntö is also attested in dialects. Alternatively, possibly borrowed from Sami, from Proto-Samic *sovōn.
Probably an alteration of earlier slang sönderi, from Swedish sönder. Alternatively possibly from Swedish söcken.

parole.significato: sousem, Canadian stud, Scandinavian stud (variant of stud poker)
parole.testo: Named after the phrase uttered by a player who passes raising the bet; possibly from English check or from French sousem. In any case probably also inspired by sökö (etymology 1).

Probably either derived from dialectal tainio + -tua, from Proto-Finnic *tainijo, or directly borrowed from Proto-Norse [Term?] (whence Swedish dåna). Alternatively, possibly from the same root as taipua.

parole.significato: an open flat area of land: field, yard
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *tandër. Equivalent to *tante- + -re. Cognate to Karelian tanner, Karelian tannar, Veps tandar, Veps tandarta (“to tread down”), Veps tandreh, Estonian tanderdada, Estonian tandermik (“playground”), Proto-Samic *tuontër (“a kind of mountain in Lapland”). Probably derived from Proto

parole.significato: waste fibres, scutching tow; tangled fibres of hemp or cotton, often with shives
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *tappura, probably from Proto-Finno-Permic *tappa. Alternatively, possibly equivalent to tappaa + -ura, from dialectal use of tappaa to signify threshing of cotton or hemp.
From Proto-Finnic *tarbit'ak. Equivalent to tarve (“need”) + -ita or alternatively, borrowed from Proto-Germanic *þarbāną + -ita. Cognate with Ingrian tarvita and Karelian tarvita.

parole.significato: saucer (small shallow dish to hold a cup and catch drips)
parole.testo: Through some way from either German Tasse (“cup with a handle”) or Low German Tass, both from Old French tasse, from Medieval Latin tassa, from Arabic طَاس (ṭās), from Middle Persian tšt'.

parole.significato: to meet (come face to face with)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *tabat'ak, probably borrowed from Proto-Germanic *dabaną. Cognate with Ingrian tavata, Karelian tavata, Votic tavatõ, Estonian tabama, Ludian tabada, Livonian ta’bbõ (“to guess, to solve a riddle”). Alternatively, sometimes compared with Erzya тавадомс (tavadoms), Udmurt тупаны (tu
Most likely borrowed from Russian тесла (tesla), from Proto-Slavic *teslò, *tesla; alternatively or partially from Swedish täxla. In either case, a liquid metathesis took place: *sl > ls.
From Proto-Finnic *tërva, borrowed from either Proto-Baltic *dérwa or Proto-Germanic *terwą, but in either case ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dérw-o-m, from *dóru (“wood”).

parole.significato: I don't think, hardly (used to express doubt, often with softening clitic -pa or -han)
parole.testo: Originates from eastern dialects; probably as a loan from Karelian toko, from dialectal Russian токо́ (tokó); alternatively from toki + -ko.
From Proto-Finnic *tuhma, possibly either from Proto-Finno-Permic *tušma or borrowed from Proto-Germanic *dusmaz.

parole.significato: thwart (seat across a boat on which a rower may sit)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *tukto, either from Proto-Uralic *tuktɜ (“cross-beam”) (compare Hungarian tat (“stern (of a ship)”), Komi-Zyrian тік (tik, “cross wood, cross bar”) and Tym Southern Selkup тати (tati, “thwart (of a ship”)), or alternatively borrowed from Proto-Germanic [Term?] (compare Old Norse þo

parole.significato: cathedral (principal church of a bishop's diocese)
parole.testo: tuomio (“judgement”) + kirkko (“church”), a mistaken calque of Swedish domkyrka (“cathedral”); the initial component dom- was interpreted as dom (“judgment”), when it actually derives from Latin domus (“home”) (compare German Dom (“cathedral”)). Alternatively, it may represent a phono-semantic match

parole.significato: A tuft of grass or other plants.
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *tup'as (compare Karelian tuvas, Ludian tubaz, Veps tupaz), possibly borrowed from Proto-Germanic *þūbaz (compare Icelandic þúfa, Swedish tuva) or from Indo-Iranian (see the Proto-Finnic entry for more).
From Proto-Finnic *vakja, borrowed either from Proto-Baltic [Term?] (compare Latvian vadzis (“crook, hook”), Lithuanian vagis) or alternatively from Proto-Germanic *wagjaz (compare English wedge).
Possibly from Proto-Finnic *vaanidak, probably borrowed from Proto-Norse [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *wēnijaną, or alternatively possibly cognate with Erzya and Moksha ваномс (vanoms, “to look”).
From Proto-Finnic *vaat'ëk, probably borrowed from Germanic, possibly from Northwest Proto-Germanic *wādiz, or alternatively a more recent borrowing (compare Old Norse váð). Displaced sopa.

parole.significato: to demand, insist, call for, order
parole.testo: Probably borrowed either from Proto-Norse [Term?] (from Proto-Germanic *wadjōną (“to wager, to pledge”)) or alternatively from Proto-Norse [Term?] (from Proto-Germanic *kwadjaną (“to greet”)). However, the -aa- (as opposed to short -a-) seems difficult to explain. Compare Karelian vuatie.
From Proto-Finnic *vaha, borrowed either from Proto-Germanic *wahsą, from Proto-Baltic *vakša (compare Latvian vasks), or all three are from a substrate language.

Most likely borrowed from Swedish valt, the supine of välja (“to choose, elect”), as in many card games the trump suit is nominated. Has also been compared with archaic Norwegian velt and Danish vælt, with dialectal variant valt in the latter, both ultimately from Old Norse velta (“to roll over, tur

parole.significato: bath broom, a kind of whip made of birch twigs and used in the sauna to enhance the effect of heat by gently beating on…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old East Slavic хвостъ (xvostŭ), or alternatively borrowed from North Germanic (compare Swedish kvast). Related to Ingrian vasta, Karelian vašta, Ludian vast and Veps vast.

From Proto-Finnic *vehmärä (cognate with Estonian vehmer and Livonian vi’emõr), possibly borrowed from Proto-Baltic [Term?] (whence Lithuanian vežimas). Such Germanic words as Old Swedish fimber stang, Swedish fimmerstång and Baltic German femer, fiemer, femerstange, fiemerstange (“shaft of a yoke”)
A nativized colloquial form of either French vingt-et-un, English twenty-one or Spanish veintiuno.

parole.significato: shoot (emerging stem and embryonic leaves of a new plant)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *vërso (compare Estonian võrsuma ~ Finnish versoa), probably borrowed from Indo-Iranian, either from Pre-Proto-Indo-Iranian *wérćos (whence Proto-Indo-Iranian *wálćas, Sanskrit वल्श (valśa, “shoot, branch”)) or Proto-Indo-Iranian *wr̥ćšás (whence Sanskrit वृक्ष (vṛkṣa, “tree”)).
Possibly borrowed from Proto-Norse [Term?], from Proto-Germanic *swinþaz (for *þ > *h, compare huopa, murha), or alternatively onomatopoeic.
From Proto-Finnic *virta, borrowed from either Proto-Slavic *vьrtъ or a Baltic cognate thereof.

parole.significato: can, to be able to, to be capable
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *voidak, either from Proto-Finno-Permic *wäjä- or from Proto-Uralic *woje-.

parole.significato: rent (payment made by a tenant or user of a service)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *vookra (compare Karelian vuokra, Ludian vuogr; no more cognates are known), borrowed from Proto-Germanic *wōkraz (“interest; usury, gain; increase”), or alternatively a more recent borrowing from Middle Low German wôker.

From Proto-Finnic *ükteksä, from Proto-Finno-Permic *ükteksä (cognate with Erzya вейксэ (vejksë), Moksha вейхкса (vejhksa)). The initial component is yksi (“one”), but the nature of the latter component (shared with kahdeksan (“eight”)) remains disputed (see the Proto-Finno-Permic entry for more). T

parole.significato: mother (woman in relation to her children)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *äitei (compare Southern Ostrobothnian äitee, äiree, Estonian eit (“old woman”), Võro äide, äidi, ääde (“mother, grandmother”)), borrowed from Proto-Germanic *aiþį̄ (compare Gothic 𐌰𐌹𐌸𐌴𐌹 (aiþei)) or from later Proto-Norse [script needed] (*aiðijōn). Attested since the time of Mikae

parole.significato: bank (edge of river or lake, especially a steep one)
parole.testo: From Proto-Finnic *äpräs, borrowed either from Proto-Germanic *auraz or alternatively from *ōferaz. Cognate with Karelian äpräs, Livvi äbräs and Ludian äbräz.
